newsitem.title: USA: Ohio budget director outlines tight finances.
newsitem.headline: Ohio budget director outlines tight finances.

text.p: Ohio Budget Director Greg Browning told the House Finance and Appropriations Committee Tuesday that the state faces a "tight fiscal situation" due to a slowing economy and previously approved tax cuts.
He said the $36.14 billion fiscal 1998-99 biennial general fund budget unveiled Monday was designed for "high performance."

"The fiscal 1998-99 budget builds on our past progress by limiting government growth and reducing state taxes in a slow growth economy where global competition requires both private and public organizations to continually reinvent themselves," Browning said.
On the education front, Browning said Gov. George Voinovich's budget calls for $300 million of funding for primary and secondary school capital improvements backed by the state.
Under the plan, $200 million would be allocated to the 10 percent lowest wealth school districts and $100 million for the state's urban school districts.

Herb Kruse, Ohio's debt coordinator, said the $300 million of bonds would be backed by annual state appropriations and would be issued through the state treasurer's office. He added that there is about $170 million of untapped previously approved bond authorization for schools remaining.
Browning said the governor was also proposing the creation of a school building authority to assist school districts in their capital needs.
Browning said the school foundation level would increase to $3,660 per pupil in fiscal 1998 from the current level of $3,500, and to $3,767 in fiscal 1999.

The budget would be less generous for higher education, with a total increase of $152.1 million or 7.7 percent proposed for the upcoming bienium. Meanwhile, tuition increases would be be capped at four percent from the current six percent, Browning said.

Browning said the proposed two-year budget would increase Medicaid spending by more than $500 million to cover projected caseload growth and inflationary increases. He added that changes in federal participation in the Medicaid program is estimated to cost Ohio $160 million during the bienium.
Voinovich's budget also calls for making permanent income tax reductions enacted last year. Those reductions would be triggered only under certain budgetary conditions.

In addition, Browning said the budget includes targeted tax reforms and reductions that would total $53.2 million in fiscal 1999. Taxes targeted would include corporate franchise, insurance and banking taxes.

The proposed budget projects a $157 million unreserved ending balance for fiscal 1997, which ends June 30, and unreserved balances of $212.5 million at the end of fiscal 1998 and $91 million at the end of fiscal 1999.

Ohio's budget stabilization fund, which currently totals more than $828 million or nearly five percent of general revenues, is projected to grow to $857.8 million at the end of fiscal 1999, according to budget documents.
